claims.quote: Constraint Handling Rules (CHR) is a high-level programming language based on multi-headed, committed-choice, guarded multiset rewrite rules.
claims.states: CHR programs are multiset rewrite rules that commit to one rule application and do not backtrack over it.

claims.quote: If there are two prime/1 constraints prime(A) and prime(B), such that B is a multiple of A, the latter constraint is removed.
claims.states: A simpagation rule deletes a matched constraint from the store when it fires.
claims.feature: facts used up when a rule reads them

claims.quote: It is necessary to do this explicitly since CHR has multiset semantics.
claims.where: §1.2 Constraint Handling Rules (leq program, idempotence rule)
claims.states: The CHR store is a multiset, so duplicate constraints stay unless a rule removes them.

claims.quote: It features a constraint store with set semantics
claims.states: One CHR variant, CHRd, uses a constraint store with set semantics, suited to tabled execution.

claims.quote: the existence of a decidable, sufficient and necessary test for confluence of terminating programs
claims.states: For terminating CHR programs there is a decidable test of confluence, the property that every derivation from a state ends in the same final state.
claims.feature: check that results are independent of rule order

claims.quote: CHR programs often rely on the execution control offered by the ωr semantics for
claims.states: Many CHR programs depend on the refined semantics, which tries rule occurrences in program order, to be correct or fast.

claims.quote: Attempting to prove a goal of the form D ⊃ G from the context (set of formulas) Γ leads to an attempt to prove the goal G in the extended context Γ ∪ {D}.
claims.states: An implication goal D => G is proved by adding D to the program context and proving G there.
claims.feature: adding facts for the duration of a goal

claims.quote: then every formula in the bounded part of the context must be used exactly once
claims.states: In the linear fragment, each formula in the bounded context must be consumed exactly once in a proof.
claims.feature: facts used up when a rule reads them

claims.quote: if a data base is held in the bounded part of a context, then querying the data base about an item makes that item unavailable elsewhere.
claims.states: Querying a linear (bounded) fact consumes it, so a plain query is not a non-destructive read.
claims.feature: reading a fact without consuming it

claims.quote: the latter must be split into disjoint contexts ∆1 and ∆2 for which G1 follows from ∆1 and G2 follows from ∆2
claims.states: Proving a multiplicative conjunction G1 ⊗ G2 requires splitting the resources into two disjoint parts, one for each conjunct.

claims.quote: Since there is an exponential number of such splits, it is important to delay the choice of a split as much as possible.
claims.states: The number of ways to split a context is exponential, so an interpreter delays the split (lazy splitting).

claims.quote: The rules in Σ are unordered, and several may apply, potentially giving rise to nondeterminism.
claims.states: Ceptre rules have no order, and when several apply the choice is nondeterministic.

claims.quote: Note that because of the replacement semantics of the rule, we need to reiterate everything on the right-hand side of the -o that we don’t want to disappear
claims.states: A Ceptre rule replaces the facts it matches, so any matched fact that should survive must be restated (or marked with $).
claims.feature: facts used up when a rule reads them

claims.quote: Linear Meld (LM) is a forward chaining logic programming language in the style of Datalog (Ullman 1990).
claims.states: LM evaluates bottom-up like Datalog while adding linear (consumable) facts.
claims.feature: Datalog-style forward chaining with consumable facts

claims.quote: If a rule uses linear facts, they are consumed and thus deleted from the database.
claims.states: Linear facts matched by a rule body are deleted from the database when the rule fires.
claims.feature: facts used up when a rule reads them

claims.quote: While linear facts may be retracted, persistent facts are always true once they are derived.
claims.states: LM keeps two kinds of facts: linear ones that rules consume and persistent ones (marked !) that stay true.

claims.quote: When a rule body is instantiated using facts from the database, facts are picked non-deterministically.
claims.states: Which facts a rule consumes is chosen nondeterministically, in an implementation-dependent order.

claims.quote: every node A will derive visited(A), regardless of the order in which rules are applied
claims.states: For the visit program on a connected graph, the authors argue the result is the same whatever order rules fire in; this is shown per program.

claims.quote: Horn-clause logic is augmented with rules, called embedded implications, which can hypothetically add atomic formulas to a rulebase.
claims.states: Embedded implications extend Horn clauses with rules that hypothetically add facts to the rulebase.
claims.feature: adding facts for the duration of a goal

claims.quote: is true if inserting C into the database makes B true
claims.states: A hypothetical rule A <- B[add: C] makes A true if B would hold after inserting C into the database.
claims.feature: adding facts for the duration of a goal

claims.quote: increases its data-complexity from PTIME to PSPACE
claims.states: Adding hypothetical additions to function-free Horn-clause logic raises its data complexity from PTIME to PSPACE.

claims.quote: When deletions are added as well, complexity increases again, to EXPTIME.
claims.states: Allowing hypothetical deletions as well raises data complexity to EXPTIME.

claims.quote: It is shown that negation does not increase complexity.
claims.states: Stratified negation-as-failure can be added to hypothetical rulebases without raising data complexity.

claims.quote: it is shown that for a given rulebase, the value of FIXPOINT is independent of the way it is stratified
claims.states: The bottom-up fixpoint of a stratified hypothetical rulebase does not depend on which stratification is used to compute it.

claims.quote: an embedded implication plays the role of assuming its premise for deriving its consequence
claims.states: In Hypothetical Datalog an embedded implication assumes its premise while deriving its conclusion.
claims.feature: adding facts for the duration of a goal

claims.quote: it lacks the ability to locally delete tuples in the same context
claims.states: The earlier tabled Hypothetical Datalog could add tuples locally for a goal but not delete them locally.
claims.feature: removing facts for the duration of a goal

claims.quote: This paper describes a method of boosting shape analyses by defining a compositional method, where each procedure is analyzed independently of its callers.
claims.states: Bi-abduction lets a shape analysis summarize each procedure without knowing its callers.

claims.quote: it jointly infers anti-frames (missing portions of state) and frames (portions of state not touched by an operation)
claims.states: Bi-abduction infers both the missing state a call needs (anti-frame) and the state it leaves untouched (frame).
claims.feature: infers missing and untouched parts of state

claims.quote: Then, if a procedure (or recursive procedure group) is changed, only it has to be re-analyzed; the old analysis results for independent procedures remain unchanged.
claims.states: A compositional analysis is incremental: changing one procedure only requires re-analyzing it.

claims.quote: it has seen over 100 thousand reported issues fixed by developers before code reaches production
claims.states: Infer's reported issues had led to over 100,000 fixes before code reached production.

claims.quote: the diff time deployment saw a 70% fix rate
claims.states: Reporting at code-review (diff) time got a 70% fix rate where a batch deployment got 0%.

claims.quote: Infer, as we will discuss, uses one analysis based on the theory of Separation Logic
claims.where: Introduction, technical overview of Infer and Zoncolan
claims.states: One of Infer's analyses is based on separation logic.
claims.feature: separation logic in a deployed analyzer

claims.quote: compositional analyses are naturally incremental—changing one procedure does not necessitate
claims.states: Because the analyses are compositional, changing one procedure does not force re-analysis of all others.

claims.quote: we use a specification form [presumption]code[result] which says that the post-assertion result be an under-approximation (subset) of the final states that can be reached starting from states satisfying the presumption
claims.states: An incorrectness triple promises that every state in its result can actually be reached.

claims.quote: Because of under-approximation, reasoning is arranged to avoid false positives (bug suggestions that are not true).
claims.states: Incorrectness logic can prove that bugs are present but not that they are absent, and is arranged to give no false positives.

claims.quote: use it to derive a begin-anywhere, intra-procedural symbolic execution analysis that has no false positives by construction
claims.states: Incorrectness separation logic yields an analysis, Pulse in Infer, that reports no false positives by construction.

claims.quote: we recover the frame rule for a refined model with negative heap assertions
claims.states: Under-approximate local reasoning needs explicit negative facts (a location is known deallocated) for the frame rule to hold.
claims.feature: negative facts needed for local reasoning

claims.quote: Informally, a judgement m |= φ ∧ ψ is a declaration that the resource m satisfies φ and satisfies ψ, meanwhile the judgement m |= φ ∗ ψ says that it can be split into two parts n and n′ such that n |= φ and n′ |= ψ.
claims.states: In BI the additive conjunction lets both sides share the same resource, while the multiplicative conjunction splits it into two parts.

claims.quote: contexts in the sequent calculus require two different context-formers: one that admits structural rules of Weakening and Contraction, and another that does not
claims.states: BI contexts combine a sharing context-former (duplicable, discardable) with a separating one that is not.

claims.quote: in the resource interpretation of BI a proposition is not a resource itself, but a declaration about the state of some resources
claims.states: Unlike linear logic, a BI proposition describes resources rather than being a resource that proof search consumes.
claims.feature: facts used up when a rule reads them

claims.quote: The equivalent implementation in hHLP would require a tagging system to show compatibility of the columns
claims.states: In a deductive-database example, BI's separating conjunction expresses 'one item from each disjoint column' that plain hereditary Harrop logic programming would need tags for.
claims.feature: separating conjunction in a deductive database

claims.quote: that asserts that P and Q hold for disjoint portions of the addressable storage
claims.states: The separating conjunction P ∗ Q asserts that P and Q hold for disjoint parts of the heap.

claims.quote: neither contraction, p ⇒ p ∗ p,nor weakening, p ∗ q ⇒ p,are sound.
claims.states: In separation logic a heap assertion cannot be duplicated (p does not imply p ∗ p) or dropped from a separating conjunction.

claims.quote: p1 ∧ p2 ⇒ p1 ∗ p2 when p1 or p2 is pure p1 ∗ p2 ⇒ p1 ∧ p2 when p1 and p2 are pure
claims.where: §3 Assertions and their Inference Rules (pure assertions)
claims.states: For pure (heap-independent) assertions the separating and ordinary conjunctions coincide.
claims.feature: conjunction over duplicable facts behaves like ordinary conjunction

claims.quote: Our implementation, which is written in Prolog to allow a declarative specification of the inference rules of the proof system
claims.states: A separation-logic entailment prover was written in Prolog so its inference rules could be stated declaratively.
claims.feature: separation-logic reasoning implemented as logic program
